analysis.one_liner: Bans most noncompete agreements that employers impose on their workers.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to ban most noncompete agreements was introduced in June 2025 with three cosponsors and has sat in the Senate labor committee since with no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The Workforce Mobility Act would make it illegal for employers to require most workers to sign noncompete agreements, which stop workers from taking a similar job with a competitor after they leave. Employers could still protect client lists and secrets with trade secret law and nondisclosure agreements, and noncompetes would remain allowed in a few narrow cases: when someone sells a business, dissolves a partnership, or is a top executive who gets a paid severance deal. The Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Labor would enforce the ban, and workers could also sue in court for damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers covered by noncompete agreements, which the bill's own findings say touch about 1 in 5 U.S. workers. They would be free to switch jobs, negotiate higher pay, or start competing businesses without legal threat. Job-switchers and workers in fields like healthcare, tech, and low-wage services, where noncompetes are common, would see the most direct gain.

how_it_helps.text: The bill voids noncompete agreements for ordinary workers, freeing them to change jobs within their field, which the bill's findings say raises wages, speeds innovation, and boosts productivity [S2].

It preserves the tools employers legitimately need: trade secret law and nondisclosure agreements remain fully available, and noncompetes still apply to people selling a business or partnership stake [S2].

Enforcement has teeth: the FTC and Labor Department can act, state attorneys general can sue, and individual workers can bring their own lawsuits for actual damages plus attorney's fees. The bill also bars employers from forcing workers into arbitration or giving up class-action rights over noncompete violations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use noncompetes to keep workers from leaving would lose that tool and would have to retain workers the old-fashioned way: with pay and conditions. Some businesses argue they would invest less in training workers whom competitors can freely hire, and lawyers expect more disputes over what counts as a trade secret.

drawbacks.text: The ban has carve-outs: noncompetes still apply when a business is sold, when a partnership dissolves, and for senior executives (top decision-makers in the highest 10% of pay) who receive a full year's salary as severance, capped at one year [S2]. Critics would call these holes; supporters call them narrow and justified.

Some employers argue trade secret and nondisclosure law is not enough to protect client relationships and investment in worker training, and that losing noncompetes would make them hesitant to train staff [S2].

The bill creates a new private right of action with attorney's fees and dual FTC/Labor Department enforcement, which could generate significant litigation while the agencies build shared enforcement standards during the first year after enactment [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary workers the upside is broad and concrete: roughly one in five workers is covered by a noncompete today, and the ban directly restores their freedom to change jobs and earn more. The costs fall mainly on employers who used noncompetes as a cheap retention tool, and the carve-outs for executives and business sales keep the most legitimate business uses intact. The design is close to what economists who study the issue recommend.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate in June 2025 and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has been sitting with no hearing or vote; the current Congress runs through January 2027, so it is not dead yet.

narrative.text: Sen. Chris Murphy introduced the Workforce Mobility Act of 2025 on June 11, 2025, joined by Sens. Todd Young, Kevin Cramer, and Tim Kaine [S1][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, and no further action has been taken [S4].
Its three cosponsors give it bipartisan sponsorship, two Republicans and one Democrat [S3].
The bill text finds that about 1 in 5 U.S. workers is covered by a noncompete agreement, and that these agreements lower wages, restrict mobility, and slow innovation [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers that rely on noncompete agreements: the ban has not advanced, so the status quo that favors them continues while the bill sits without a hearing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four Senate backers split evenly, two Democrats and two Republicans, and no one has gone on record against it; the obstacle is committee inaction, not a party fight.

industries.industry: Employers that use noncompetes (health systems, staffing, tech, franchises)
industries.note: The bill strips them of agreements covering roughly one in five workers, forcing them to retain staff through pay and conditions instead of legal threats. Their interest in keeping noncompetes runs directly against workers' freedom to change jobs [S2].

Noncompetes stay fully legal when someone sells a business or partnership stake, and top executives with a year's severance can still be bound for up to a year. The most common uses in high-level dealmaking survive the ban [S2].

industries.industry: Staffing and recruiting firms and competing employers
industries.note: They gain a larger pool of candidates who can legally switch jobs without litigation risk, which is the same gain workers get from the ban [S2].

analysis.trajectory: Labor bills referred to the Senate HELP Committee typically get a markup and floor vote only if leadership prioritizes them; with no hearing scheduled and a modest cosponsor list, the bill will most likely sit until the Congress ends in January 2027. Versions of this bill have been reintroduced across several Congresses, so a fresh attempt in the next Congress is plausible if a chamber takes it up.
